sentences.text: Peloneustes was a medium-sized marine reptile reaching a total length of 3.5 to 4 meters, featuring a large, triangular skull that comprised about one-fifth of its body.
The front of its skull was elongated into a narrow snout equipped with conical teeth that had circular cross-sections and vertical ridges on all sides.
Unlike modern sea turtles, this animal had a short neck consisting of only 19 to 21 cervical vertebrae.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was discovered by geologist Henry Porter in a clay pit near Peterborough, England, and later purchased by Adam Sedgwick in 1866 for the University of Cambridge.
Harry Govier Seeley first described the animal as Plesiosaurus philarchus in 1869, before Richard Lydekker elevated it to its own genus in 1889.
Peloneustes swam using a method called subaqueous flight with its flippers and likely caught fish by swinging its narrow snout quickly to pierce them with sharp teeth.
Andrews hypothesized in 1913 that the tail morphology stiffened the tail to support large hind limbs and speculated it supported a small tail fin-like structure.
The valid species of the genus Peloneustes is Peloneustes philarchus, which was previously known by the synonyms Plesiosaurus philarchus, Thaumatosaurus philarchus, and Pliosaurus philarchus.

Seeley named the species Plesiosaurus sterrodeirus in the same publication where he named Peloneustes philarchus, and Lydekker later reclassified both Plesiosaurus sterrodeirus and Pleiosaurus aequalis into the genus Peloneustes.
Peloneustes lived during the Middle Jurassic period in what is now Great Britain.
Fossils are found in the Callovian-aged Peterborough Member of the Oxford Clay Formation, an inland sea approximately 30 to 50 meters deep.

There is a debate regarding the relationships of pliosaurids; White (1940) suggested they were close relatives of Elasmosauridae, while Welles (1943) argued they were more similar to Polycotylidae. The phylogenetic position of Peloneustes within Pliosauridae is debated, with O'Keefe (2001) placing it as a basal member outside a specific group, while Smith and Dyke (2008) identified it as the sister taxon to Pliosaurus. It is debated whether Peloneustes is a close relative of Pliosaurus or a basal pliosaurid within Thalassophonea, though the latter view has more support.
